ed.location: Directorate of Trade, Commerce & Industry, Lamphelpat, Imphal, Manipur

remarks: Building Plan Approval is interconnected with factory-related approvals, particularly where a factory is being established or an existing facility is being expanded.
The approval process involves Town Planning verification, technical scrutiny, inspection, permit fee payment and final approval.

findings.text: The Building Plan Approval process has shifted from the earlier manual process to the online OBPS system, converted to online processing around the previous year/December.
The process is not completely free of physical intervention; physical site inspection and technical verification continue to form part of the approval process despite digitization.

Only around five or six architects are actively capable of preparing and submitting digital building plans through OBPS, creating a bottleneck since applications must be submitted through registered architects.
The architect also undertakes follow-up with different departments on behalf of the applicant, increasing intermediary dependence.
Officials indicated Building Plan Approval generally takes 10-15 days in most cases, with a maximum of approximately 30 days also mentioned during the discussion.
Where deficiencies or queries are raised, applicants may be given up to 30 days to provide the required clarification or correction, extending the effective timeline.
The actual permit fee amount or fee structure based on building size/use/category was not specified during the discussion.

Officials discussed a risk-based classification to reduce physical inspection requirements for low-risk applications and rely more on digital verification, while retaining stronger scrutiny for higher-risk cases.
Train more registered architects on OBPS to address the shortage of architects capable of preparing and submitting digital building plans.
Adopt risk-based inspection and reduce physical inspections for eligible low-risk building applications.
Improve inter-departmental integration so that applications do not require extensive sequential follow-up across different authorities.
Improve the online checklist to ensure applicants and architects are aware of all documentation and technical requirements before submission.
Strengthen OBPS capacity and user support so that the benefits of digitization are not constrained by limited technical expertise among registered architects.
Building Plan Approval is interconnected with factory-related approvals, particularly where a factory is being established or an existing facility expanded.
Officials identified a risk-based approach (low-risk/high-risk categories) and digital verification using photographs/videos as potential improvements for suitable low-risk cases.

gaps.text: Exact permit fee amount or fee structure by building size/use/category not given in the discussion.
ED itself did not specify the validity period of the BPA/permit; the 3-year figure in the report is drawn from the 2025 Manipur municipal building bye-laws rather than from officials directly.

Risk-based classification criteria (what specifically qualifies a building as low-risk vs high-risk) were discussed in principle but not defined with specific thresholds.
Shift from a fully manual process to the OBPS online submission-and-processing system, cutting down manual paperwork for the application stage.

Proposed risk-based inspection and expanded digital verification (photos/videos) to reduce physical inspection burden for low-risk applications, alongside architect training to relieve the OBPS capacity bottleneck.

remarks: Discussion emphasized the need to balance Ease of Doing Business with regulatory compliance and safety requirements.
Factory License is interconnected with other factory-related approvals, making coordination and integration important for reducing the overall compliance burden.

findings.text: The Factory Licence process has recently transitioned from the earlier manual/physical process to an online application system.
Physical inspection remains part of the process for new Factory Licence applications despite digitization of the application step, so the service is only partially online.
The only timeline figure stated (90 days) is described in terms matching Factory Building Plan Approval (construction/extension permission), not a distinct Factory Licence issuance timeline.
The Factory Licence is valid for 10 years with an auto-renewal provision under the Manipur Factories Rules, 2021.
The Factory Licence fee is variable based on worker count and installed horsepower, but exact fee figures were not given in the discussion.

No official Manipur source was identified establishing deemed approval for Factory Licence, despite the Manipur Factories Rules, 2021 and Public Services Delivery Guarantee Act, 2021 being relevant frameworks.
A detailed post-approval compliance checklist was not discussed, though maintenance of registers, periodic testing, and equipment upkeep were mentioned as general post-approval obligations.

Officials discussed risk-based classification (low/medium/high risk) to reduce inspection for low-risk establishments while retaining stronger verification for higher-risk ones, though specific classification criteria were not given.

Factory Licence is part of a sequence of interconnected approvals (Building Plan Approval, Factory Building Plan Approval, Factory Licence, Consent to Establish, Consent to Operate, occupancy-related approvals), and no specific Act or Rule driving individual requirements was identified.
Introduce a risk-based inspection approach so eligible low-risk establishments can be subject to simplified verification.
Operationalize self-certification for eligible categories of factories, a framework already under implementation as a reform.
Increase use of accredited third-party agencies for eligible inspections to reduce the burden on departmental inspection teams.
Renewal of Factory Licence is processed online and generally does not require routine physical inspection.
Integrate factory-related approvals to reduce multiple departmental interactions and repeated submission of information.
The discussion emphasized the need to balance Ease of Doing Business with regulatory compliance and safety requirements.

Exact fee amounts or fee bands by worker-count/horsepower were not given — only that the fee is variable based on these two parameters.

findings.text: Digital submission is available for Factory Building Plan Approval — the building plan is submitted through an online system/portal.
Only a limited number of architects are currently capable of preparing and submitting plans through the digital system, creating a capacity constraint.
Architects undertake submission and follow-up with the concerned departments, increasing intermediary dependence.
The process involves coordination with multiple authorities and includes physical verification/inspection, so it is only partially online.

The Manipur EoDB portal lists Factory Permit and Factory Licence as separate approvals, so the broader EoDB document checklist should not automatically be treated as the document list for Factory Building Plan Approval itself — creating potential confusion over required documents.

A 90-day timeline applies for Factory Building Plan Approval, covering construction, extension, or taking a building into use as a factory, per the Manipur Factories Rules, 2021 and Manipur Public Services Delivery Guarantee Act, 2021.
The prescribed fee for FBPA is based on factory category, size, worker strength, or machinery/power capacity, but exact fee figures were not specified.
FBPA approval usually has no fixed validity period and remains applicable to the approved construction/extension plan, subject to the conditions of the approval.

Factory establishment requires multiple linked approvals (BPA/FBPA, Factory Licence, Consent to Establish, Consent to Operate), leading to repeated submission and verification of project-related information across departments.
Introduce a single-window mechanism or nodal agency for factory-related approvals to reduce multiple departmental interactions.
Adopt a risk-based inspection approach, reducing physical inspection requirements for eligible low-risk cases.
Train and onboard more architects on the online building plan approval system to reduce dependence on the limited pool of trained architects.
Reduce repeated submission of information by enabling departments to access information already submitted during earlier approvals.
Expand self-certification and third-party inspection for eligible cases while retaining appropriate scrutiny for high-risk projects.

remarks: Officials emphasized the need to balance Ease of Doing Business with fire-safety and public-safety requirements.
Delays can occur when applicants have not fulfilled the required fire-safety conditions or need to provide additional clarification/documents.

findings.text: The Fire NOC process is not entirely online; it involves both application/administrative processing and physical inspection by the Fire Department.
Third-party agencies can conduct a pre-inspection before the application/departmental inspection stage, helping identify fire-safety deficiencies at an earlier stage.
Officials indicated a prescribed seven-day timeline for Fire NOC, with some NOCs issued within two days where documentation and compliance were already complete.
Where deficiencies are identified, additional time is required for the applicant to undertake corrective measures and for the department to conduct follow-up verification.
Fees vary based on plinth area, height and occupancy type, calculated per square meter under state guidelines; exact figures were not given in the discussion.

A final Fire NOC/Fire Safety Certificate from the Manipur Fire Service is typically valid for 1 year and requires annual re-inspection and renewal before expiry; this is not specified on the official Manipur EoDB service information itself.
No deemed approval exists for Fire NOC; the Fire Department does not currently provide automatic/deemed approval as part of the process.

Applications are categorized into low, medium and high risk; for low-risk cases physical inspection may not be required where third-party inspection, photos/videos and other verification are already completed.
Physical inspection was identified as the principal compliance burden for Fire NOC.
Apply a risk-based inspection approach, reducing departmental physical inspections for eligible low-risk establishments.
Provide a comprehensive online checklist of fire-safety requirements so applicants can ensure compliance before submission, reducing incomplete applications.
Strengthen the use of accredited third-party agencies to verify fire-safety compliance before the departmental inspection stage.
Operationalize self-certification for eligible low-risk categories, supported by appropriate risk-based verification.
Improve online integration of the Fire NOC process to reduce manual interactions while retaining necessary safety checks.
Officials emphasized the need to balance Ease of Doing Business with fire-safety and public-safety requirements.

Risk-classification criteria (precisely what qualifies as low/medium/high risk) for Fire NOC were not detailed.

Use of third-party pre-inspection agencies to identify fire-safety deficiencies before departmental inspection/application stage, and faster issuance (within two days) observed for fully-compliant applicants.
